findings.location: Results para 1 vs Measures, Engaging communication; Table 1 Communication row
findings.quote: Measures: 'response options 1 = Needs a lot of work, 2 = Needs a little work, 3 = Good, 4 = Outstanding; Cronbach's alpha =0.93'. Results: 'the mean level of engaging communication was 3.83 on a 1.25 -5 scale, corresponding to "good" for such facets as frequency.' Table 1: 'Communication (mean, SD) | 3.83 (0.42)'.
findings.notes: The paper states two mutually exclusive scale ranges for its lead predictor. The Measures section defines four response options topping out at 4 = 'Outstanding'; the Results section describes the same variable as sitting on a '1.25-5 scale'. Under the Measures reading, NO coalition can exceed 4, so the proportion above 4 is necessarily 0/64; the tool shows that is very hard to reconcile with mean 3.83 / SD 0.42 (expected 34.3% above 4, binomial p = 3.0e-12). The interpretive gloss compounds the conflict: on a 1-4 scale a mean of 3.83 sits between 'Good' and 'Outstanding', much nearer the latter, yet the text glosses it as 'good' - which reads naturally only on a 1-5 scale. I have DOWNGRADED the tool's own 'highly_suspicious' to 'suspicious' because the test assumes normality, and a ceiling-bounded aggregate would be left-skewed, which weakens (though does not remove) the inference. Note also that check_sd_range finds SD 0.42 admissible under BOTH readings, so dispersion alone does not resolve which scale is correct. This is a documentary contradiction between two stated constraints, not an invented bound; it warrants clarification because it changes how the headline predictor should be interpreted.

findings.location: Table 2, Constant row, column 1 (Poisson model with Communication as predictor)
findings.reproduction: metascience statcheck --text "Constant column 1: z = 3.01, p < .001. Constant column 1 most favourable rounding: z = 3.02, p < .001."
findings.notes: The z was produced by check_regression (t = B/SE = -4.51/1.50 = -3.0067), an MCP-only tool with no CLI form; statcheck then recomputed p. Reported 'p<.001' but the coefficient and its SE imply p = .0026, about 2.6x the claimed threshold. I deliberately also tested the most favourable rounding of the printed 2-dp inputs (z = 3.02), which still gives p = .0025, so the discrepancy is NOT explained by rounding - statcheck's own correct_at_printed_precision field returns false. This is an intercept, not a substantive claim, so it changes no conclusion; it is a reporting error.

findings.notes: The p-value column for this cell reads literally '0'. A p-value is never exactly zero. Confirmed identically in the clean markdown extraction and in the PDF, so this is not a transcription artefact. findings.location: Table 3, Number of EBP at baseline row, all three columns
findings.reproduction: metascience statcheck --text "Number of EBP at baseline column 1: z = 5.00, p = .01. Number of EBP at baseline column 3: z = 5.00, p < .001."
findings.notes: Columns 1 and 3 print an IDENTICAL coefficient and SE (0.01, 0.002) yet report p = .01 and p < .001 respectively - the same inputs cannot give both. At the point estimate z = 5.00 implies p = 1e-6, so the '.01' in column 1 is off by roughly four orders of magnitude and statcheck flags it. IMPORTANT COUNTERWEIGHT, which is why I hold this at 'suspicious' and not higher: the coefficient is printed to only ONE significant figure (0.01), so its rounding interval [0.005, 0.015] against an SE interval of [0.0015, 0.0025] admits z anywhere from 2.0 to 10.0, and p = .01 IS reachable inside that range. The real problem here is uninformative reported precision - as printed, this row cannot be verified at all - compounded by three different p-values attached to essentially one printed estimate.

findings.location: Analyses section; Tables 2-4 key predictor rows
findings.quote: Variables were retained in the fi nal models as covariates only if bivariate associations had p values under 0.10.
findings.reproduction: Not independently reproducible as a tool call: no validated multiplicity tool is exposed in this toolset. The inputs are the nine primary p-values transcribed from Tables 2-4 and verified via `metascience statcheck`.
findings.notes: Nine primary tests are run (three leadership measures x three outcomes) with no correction stated, and covariates are additionally selected by a data-driven bivariate screen at p<0.10. The five nominally significant primary results have p-values between .01 and .03; none would survive a Bonferroni-type adjustment across the nine-test family. I am flagging the ABSENCE of a stated correction, which is a design/reporting observation - it is not an arithmetic error and is entirely ordinary in this literature. The Bonferroni figure is context only and was not produced by a tool.

findings.location: Table 1, Number of coalition members row
findings.notes: RECORDED AS A NEAR-MISS FALSE ACCUSATION. On the first pass, check_table returned 'impossible' for both GRIMMER and SPRITE on this row. Inspecting the methodology strings showed why: I had declared no upper bound for coalition size, so the tools fell back to a DEFAULT 1-7 scale, on which a mean of 35.78 is trivially out of range. The granularity test had actually passed (grim_consistent: true); only the range test failed, and on an assumed bound. Re-run with a defensible bound, the row is fully GRIM- and GRIMMER-consistent and a valid integer sample exists. The paper states no maximum coalition size, so no range-based claim should be made about this row at all.

findings.quote: including coalitions without EBPs increased the sample size and hence statistical power and consistency of the estimates
findings.notes: The paper states no a-priori power analysis, so verify_power_analysis has nothing to reproduce and was not run - that absence is itself the reporting finding. For context only, required_n shows that detecting a moderate association (r = 0.30) at 80% power would need 85 units, against the 64 coalitions actually analysed. The comparison is indicative rather than exact, since the coalition-level models are Poisson and negative binomial with six covariates, not a simple correlation. The paper does invoke power informally to justify retaining zero-EBP coalitions.

unchecked.location: Table 4, all three null results (Communication B=0.53 SE=0.60; IDM B=-0.05 SE=0.98; ICR B=-0.10 SE=0.72)
unchecked.reason: The paper's headline null claim - 'none of the inclusive leadership practices that we examined was associated with subsequent EBP fidelity' - could not be evaluated with absence_of_evidence because the paper reports NO confidence intervals anywhere, and that tool requires ci_low/ci_high. Deriving a CI from B and SE would be interval arithmetic performed by hand, which is barred. This is a substantive gap: on a 1-7 fidelity scale, standard errors of 0.60-0.98 around estimates near zero are wide, so the data are compatible with effects that would be practically meaningful in either direction, yet the paper states the null without quantifying that uncertainty. No SESOI is stated either, so equivalence could not have been claimed even with intervals.

unchecked.location: Effect sizes for all nine primary tests
unchecked.reason: check_effect_plausibility could not be run because the paper explicitly declines to report standardized effect sizes: 'Results in Tables 2-4 are shown as coefficients, and do not include effect sizes, as effects are multiplicative and unit increases in key independent variables are idiosyncratic and scale-dependent.' Poisson/negative-binomial log coefficients on idiosyncratic Likert units cannot be benchmarked against the empirical field distributions the tool uses without a units mismatch.

unchecked.location: Baseline balance across the randomized Coalition Check-Up TA arms
unchecked.reason: csf_test and bayesian_table1_dispersion were not run because the paper reports no by-arm baseline table and no baseline p-values. Table 1 has a single 'All coalitions' column. Although half of the 68 coalitions were randomly assigned to the Check-Up TA, the randomized comparison is never described, so there is nothing for a baseline-similarity test to consume. Recorded rather than forced: running either tool would have required inventing the arm-level data.

parse_table warned of an ambiguous thousands/decimal separator and parse_cells_typed mis-typed the cell as estimate_ci (low=108, high=353). The row label does establish it as mean/SD, but it is an unbounded continuous-scale population count with no stated range, so GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE are all inapplicable and check_sd_range has no defensible bound. The SD exceeding the mean is unremarkable for a right-skewed population variable.

Typed as 'ambiguous' by parse_cells_typed and additionally lacking a resolvable denominator. Logged in full as finding ebp_adherence_cell_ambiguous; repeated here because no forensic tool was run on it.

unchecked.location: Reliability and association coefficients: Cronbach's alpha 0.93 (communication) and 0.88 (inclusive decision making); item correlations 0.76 (fidelity) and 0.80 (inclusion of community residents); unconditional ICC 0.10 for fidelity
unchecked.reason: No validated tool in this toolset verifies internal-consistency or reliability coefficients from summary statistics alone; doing so would require the item covariance matrix, which is not reported. All five values are in ordinary ranges and none is out of bounds on its face.

unchecked.location: Survey response rates: 60% (1108/1851) in Year 1 and 56% (945/1695) in Year 2
unchecked.reason: Both percentages are printed to zero decimals against denominators near 1700-1850, where GRIM has effectively no discriminating power - almost any numerator passes - so grim_percentage would return a vacuous 'consistent'. Verifying the specific numerator-to-percentage division is plain arithmetic with no tool that performs it, so it was not asserted either way.

unchecked.location: Supporting Information S1, Tables S1 and S2 (registry hierarchy used to classify programs as EBPs)
unchecked.reason: Referenced by the paper but not supplied with the PDF or the markdown body, so the EBP coding rules that determine the primary outcome could not be inspected.

unchecked.location: Sensitivity analyses omitting coalitions without EBPs
unchecked.reason: The paper states 'Sensitivity analyses omitting these coalitions yielded very similar associations to those reported here' but reports no numbers from them. With no coefficients, standard errors or p-values, there is nothing to check.

unchecked.location: STALT direction check on the two 'p<.001' claims (Table 2 Constant col 1; Table 3 CTC col 1)
unchecked.reason: stalt_check was run on both (calculated_p 0.002612 and 0.001282 against threshold p<0.001) and returned 'consistent' in each case, but that verdict is a DIRECTION ARTEFACT and must not be read as endorsing the threshold claims. STALT detects p-values suspiciously SMALLER than a stated threshold; here the recomputed p-values are LARGER than the threshold (the tool's own orders_of_magnitude_smaller field is negative, -0.42 and -0.11). The tool is simply not built for this direction, so its output carries no information about these cells. statcheck is the authority for them and its results are logged separately.
